text.p: Following are some of the main stories in Dutch newspapers today. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
HET FINANCIEELE DAGBLAD
- The Netherlands will veto EU policy paper on drugs, if it calls for harmonisation of legislation of member states. (p1)
- Retailer Ahold reports 54 pct higher Q3 net, boosted by U.S. supermarket chain Stop & Shop. (p1)
- Dutch consumer confidence drops sharply in November, reversing six straight months of gains. (p1)
- Shares of Amsterdam Stock Exchange pressured by profit taking. (p1)
- Transport group Nedlloyd Q3 earnings slip to Dfl 37 million (53); company forecasts modest full year profit rise. (p3)
- Ahrend, office supplies, is expecting to take over Germany's Papier Baum this year. (p3)
- Neways Electronics forecasts flat 1996 net, partly due to problems at its German subsidiary PMA. (p5)
- Brewer Heineken beats rival Grolsch in summer beer sales in Poland. (p5)
DE VOLKSKRANT
- Justice ministry is working on new procedure for doctors to report euthanasia. (p1)
- Merger of all local utility companies into a national one seems to fail, as Amsterdam fears higher electricity prices. (p2)
- Contractor Volker Stevin in cooperation with Italian company develops mini-underground train for cities. (p2)
- Royal Dutch Airlines/KLM scraps four unprofitable lines to Africa and Asia. (p33)
DE TELEGRAAF

- Amsterdam extends its existing underground-net with a new line, connecting the north with the south of the city. (p1) - Labour, originally fiercely opposed to night flights for Beek Airport, criticised in parliament for its 180 degrees turn in favour of night flights. (p8)
- Atmosphere around bankrupt aircraft maker Fokker very gloomy. (p37)
- Dutch banks row with government about free information telephone for Euro conversion. (p37)
TROUW
- Paper maker KNP BT tired of having its name confused with KPN Dutch PTT; court sentence expected on Jan. 15. (p7)
ALGEMEEN DAGBLAD
- Cable operator Casema considers bourse launch. (p12)
- Consumers association calls banks' plans to have consumers pay for costs arising from changing from national currency to Euro system, outrageous. (p13)
